1970 Plymouth Satellite "Superbird" Was $100K, Buyer Drove 3,000 Miles, Asks 145k Six Months Later
68 photos
Photo: Chrome Cars
Chrysler engineers spent thousands of hours inside wind tunnels during 1969 to make the 1970 Plymouth Road Runner Superbird splice the atmosphere at 200 mph, which meant a folding fabric roof was completely out of the question. Yet, sitting inside the Phoenix showroom of Streetside Classics in Mesa, Arizona, is the ultimate Mopar contradiction: a 1970 Plymouth B-body with a nose cone, a rear wing, and no roof in between them. It’s a Bird? It’s a plane? No, it’s not Superbird/man, but a Satellite.
In period NASCAR competition, a hypothetical drag-inducing soft top would have shredded at high speed, and the towering rear wing was specifically engineered to brace against rigid quarter panels above a flush-mounted rear window plug. This custom build embraces that mechanical paradox with a pointed nose cone, concealed headlights, front fender air extractors, exposed chrome hood pins, white side strobes, and a black vinyl top fitted with a glass rear window.
Beneath the pinned hood sits a non-original 440-cubic-inch V8 upgraded with Indy aluminum cylinder heads and a Holley four-barrel carburetor, coupled via an A727 TorqueFlite 3-speed automatic transmission to an 8.75-inch rear axle. The chassis features Hotchkis suspension, tubular upper control arms, subframe connectors, drilled and slotted front disc brakes, Dynomax dual exhaust, 15-inch Rallye wheels on 275/60R15 BFGoodrich tires, and a white vinyl bucket-seat interior with a console.
To understand the hows and whys circumvoluting the very existence of this open-air aero warrior wannabe, let’s glance at the humble B-body platform that donated its bones: the Plymouth Satellite. Introduced for the 1965 model year and produced across three distinct generations through 1974, the Satellite debuted as the flagship trim of the intermediate Belvedere line – the rootstock on which all Plymouth mid-sizer scions were grafted in the sixties.
Photo: Chrome Cars First-generation models ran from 1965 to 1967 and were offered strictly as two-door hardtops and convertibles equipped with standard vinyl bucket seats.
The second generation spanned 1968 to 1970, expanding the Satellite into a family series with four-door sedans, station wagons, and the upscale Sport Satellite sub-series, before the fuselage-styled third generation carried the badge from 1971 until the mid-size Fury replaced it in 1975. While this family tree would induce the impression that the Satellite was mostly a grocery getter, the moniker has some very high-horse rights to sit among the legendary Mopar muscle cars .
The most potent factory-badged Satellite ever built was the 1966 Street Hemi variant, packing a 426-cubic-inch dual-quad V8 rated at 425 horsepower and 490 lb-ft of torque. Mother Mopar’s emblematic powerhouse wasn’t only for Road Runners and Coronets (the two monikers to sport the most abundant production numbers of the nefarious big-block), but also for Satellites and Belvederes. At least, that’s what it was in the beginning.
Photo: Chrome Cars After Plymouth spun off the big-block GTX in 1967 and the budget-minded Road Runner in 1968, the Satellite focused on mainstream versatility, recording 82,654 total units for the 1970 model year. Not too bad, considering the total mid-size production of 158,000 units for the cheapest ChryCo division at the debut of the seventies.
Standard RH-series Satellite domestic deliveries comprised 38,129 four-door sedans, 28,200 two-door hardtops, 4,204 six-passenger station wagons, 3,277 nine-passenger station wagons, and just 701 two-door convertibles, while the upscale RP-series Sport Satellite added 8,749 hardtops, 3,010 sedans, and 3,624 wagons. In other words, the one-of-zero example you see in the gallery is built on the rarest Plymouth body style of them all for 1970. It’s something.
That year, Satellite buyers could choose between a standard 145-horsepower 225-cube Slant Six with a single-barrel carburetor, a 230-horsepower 318 two-barrel V8, a 290-horsepower 383-CID two-barrel V8, or a top-spec 330-horsepower 383-cubic-inch four-barrel V8. Transmission choices included a standard 3-speed manual, an optional 4-speed manual, or a 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic.
Photo: Chrome Cars A 1970 Satellite convertible carried a base price of $2,970 with the Slant Six or $3,060 with the standard-issue 318 V8.
Conversely, the 1970 Plymouth Road Runner Superbird occupied the opposite end of the Mopar spectrum, engineered to satisfy NASCAR homologation rules and lure Richard Petty back to the Plymouth camp from Ford.
Unlike the multi-variant Satellite, the Superbird was offered in a single RM23 two-door hardtop body style topped by a mandatory vinyl roof to conceal the rear window plug welds, carrying a factory base price of $4,298 before options.
When NASCAR raised its homologation requirement from 500 cars to one unit per two Plymouth dealers for 1970, the division produced at least 1,935 Superbirds. Every example packed a big-block V8 paired with either a 4-speed manual or a 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic, resulting in 824 manuals and 1,084 automatic transmissions installed across the domestic run.
Photo: Chrome Cars At the base of the Superbird hierarchy sat the U-code 375-horsepower 440-4 Super Commando V8, which accounted for 1,084 cars split between 626 TorqueFlite automatics and 458 manuals.
Next came the V-code 390-horsepower 440 Six-Barrel V8 with three twos (two-barrel carburetors) at 716 units, comprising 408 automatics and 308 three-pedals, while the 425-horsepower R-code 426-cubic-inch Street Hemi totaled 135 cars: 77 automatics and 58 row-your-owns.
With authentic hardtop Superbirds commanding steep six-figure, and exceptional examples going into seven figures, and an open-air factory version never having existed, a builder decided to merge Plymouth's rarest 1970 B-body drop-top with its wildest aero package . According to its VIN, (RH27C0G208913) this car rolled off the St. Louis, Missouri assembly line in 1970 as one of those 701 Satellite convertibles, originally equipped with a C-code 225-cubic-inch Slant-Six engine under the hood.
Photo: Chrome Cars Swapping that economy-oriented six-cylinder for a 440-cubic-inch V8 and grafting on the winged nose-and-tail kit birthed this custom tribute, which shows 42,187 miles on the odometer, and $144,995 on its asking price tag. Asan added curiosity, note that this car offered for sale (and subsequently sold) earlier this year by a German dealership , with an asking price of €89,000 (about $99k), and with 39,916 miles on the clock.
According to the German listing, the wing comes from an original Superbird, and the fenders are also original (they didn’t specify which fenders, namely the ones holding the wing, or the front ones). Rest of the Superbird lookalike details (nose cone, pop-up headlights, air scoops are reproductions crafted by a Superbird specialist.
I know some would consider it a blasphemy, while other, more understanding gearheads will appreciate the workmanship. Which side are you one? There’s a comment section for that answer, feel free to use it.
